title: Applying & Diffing Manifests
intro: Typing one-off imperative commands (like earlier tutorials) is great for learning and quick fixes, but real infrastructure lives in version-controlled YAML files applied declaratively.

steps.prompt: Apply a manifest file 'deployment.yaml' to the cluster.
steps.explanation: apply is declarative — it compares the file to the cluster's current state and only changes what's different, unlike 'create' which fails if the object already exists.
steps.why: Every imperative command from earlier tutorials ('kubectl create deployment', 'kubectl scale'...) has a YAML+apply equivalent — apply is what you'd actually use in CI/CD since it's repeatable and diffable.

steps.prompt: Before applying a change, preview exactly what would be different.
steps.explanation: This shows a diff against the live cluster state without changing anything — a safety check before you actually apply.
steps.why: This is the closest thing kubectl has to a dry-run-with-explanation — '--dry-run=client' would validate the file, but diff specifically shows what would CHANGE versus what's live right now.

steps.prompt: Apply every YAML file in the './manifests/' directory at once.
steps.fake_output:
deployment.apps/web configured
service/web unchanged
configmap/app-config unchanged
steps.explanation: Pointing -f at a directory applies every manifest inside it — 'unchanged' means that particular object already matched, so nothing happened to it.
steps.why: This is how most teams actually deploy — one 'apply -f ./manifests/' rather than remembering and re-running a dozen individual imperative commands.

steps.prompt: Back up the current live state of the 'web' deployment to a file before making a risky change.
expected_commands: kubectl get deployment web -o yaml > backup.yaml
steps.fake_output: (no terminal output — the deployment's current spec was written to backup.yaml)
steps.explanation: This captures the exact current spec as YAML, so if a change goes wrong you have something concrete to apply back.
steps.why: This isn't a real substitute for actual version control (git), but it's a fast, no-setup safety net for a risky one-off change made outside your normal GitOps flow.
